This question will resolve as **Yes** if any of the following happens after December 31, 2024 before January 1, 2026:

* A New Drug Application (NDA) for the treatment of a mental disorder (as defined by the [Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Illnesses](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/articles/24291-diagnostic-and-statistical-manual-dsm-5), the DSM-5) is filed to the FDA for a psychedelic.
* An application for an Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) for the treatment of a mental disorder (as defined by the DSM-5) is filed to the FDA for a psychedelic.
* The DEA reschedules any psychedelic under the U.S. Controlled Substances Act to a less restrictive schedule (e.g., from Schedule I to Schedule II).

For the purposes of this questions, a psychedelic is defined broadly and includes:

* psychedelic indolealkylamines(e.g. LSD, psilocybin, DMT)
* psychedelic phenylethylamines (e.g. mescaline, MDMA, the 2C series)

**New Hope for Mental Health: Can Psychedelic Substances Be a Breakthrough?**
The European Commission is already taking action. The study is generating high expectations. The question is: can psychedelic substances really be a new frontier in treating many mental illnesses? Commonly known as drugs, they are illegal and stigmatized, but in therapeutic doses and always associated with psychotherapy, they could be a breakthrough? The University of Trento, with the first Italian conference on the topic, promoted by the Department of Psychology and Cognitive Sciences, asked this question last year. The conference broke a taboo. Following the many clinical trials conducted abroad, which seem to demonstrate their effectiveness, a specific scientific society, Simepsi, was born in Italy about a year ago, led by psychiatrist Mauro D'Alonzo, which deals with training and research on psychedelic medicine. 'If the law passes also in the Senate, it will be the first EU country to introduce them in therapeutic protocols,' says Caterina Bartoli, a doctor and member of Simepsi. In Australia, psilocybin and MDMA are already approved and prescribable. The first is also authorized in New Zealand, while in Switzerland it is regularly used on request from psychiatrists after the green light from a specific commission. 'In reality, the use of these psychoactive substances has a millennial history,' says Tania Re, a psychotherapist and anthropologist who also works in Switzerland in collaboration with psychiatrists. 'It's a history linked to the culture of many indigenous communities and passed down orally from generation to generation. It's crucial to continue to investigate their safety and efficacy, the neurobiological mechanisms and the optimal procedures for a safe and replicable therapy.' 'There are many advanced studies, particularly in the United States and the United Kingdom - explains Bartoli - with a strong increase in scientific publications on the subject. In the US, the phase III of a study on the efficacy of MDMA in treating post-traumatic stress disorder has just been concluded, conducted by the scientific society Maps and the pharmaceutical company Lykos.' The Food and Drug Administration, the US regulatory agency, has asked for further data, although a 70% efficacy has already been demonstrated with just three administrations. In the UK, depression is the focus. In this field, the study by the pharmaceutical giant Compass Pathways, which has also reached phase III, is worth mentioning. The study on the treatment with psilocybin, which would validate the effectiveness of the psychedelic substance, compared to a traditional antidepressant, with a single administration, is being conducted under strict medical control, also to manage any potential side effects, such as headaches, nausea, and increased blood pressure. 'Effects that generally resolve within 24 hours,' continues Bartoli. In Italy, the only substance with psychedelic effects authorized is esketamine, a derivative of ketamine, commonly used in operating rooms. It is used by psychiatrists in the form of a nasal spray. In the US, it is used for treatment-resistant depression and suicidal ideation, while in Italy only for treatment-resistant depression. Since 2017, thanks to a ministerial decree, the use of psychedelic substances is allowed only in exceptional and compassionate cases. However, they are never prescribed. 'On the one hand, there is still a lack of knowledge in the field among our doctors, on the other hand, the molecules with psychoactive effects are still perceived as recreational drugs, to get a high,' observes Bartoli. From here, the initiative of the Luca Coscioni association, which has launched an appeal to the government, signed by 170 doctors, researchers, and psychotherapists, to allow the use of these experimental treatments. An appeal accompanied by a signature collection, promoted together with Simepsi, to ask the European Commission to fund research on psychedelics. 'The resistances are not only of an ideological type: a part of the medical class remains anchored to traditional medicine based on psychopharmaceuticals,' says Marco Perduca, coordinator of all the activities of the association related to psychoactive substances.
